questions.title: Under Minn. Stat. § 181.101, can a private employee ever recover “average daily wage” penalties, or are they exclusive to the Commissioner despite § 181.171’s “other appropriate relief” language?
questions.question_body: The court holds that only the Commissioner may “charge and collect” penalties under § 181.101(a), even though § 181.171, subd. 1 authorizes private suits for violations of § 181.101 and allows “compensatory damages and other appropriate relief,” plus “the civil penalties or damages provided for in the section violated.” How do these provisions fit together? If § 181.101 contains an average-daily-wage penalty but assigns enforcement to the Commissioner, does § 181.171 categorically bar private plaintiffs from obtaining that penalty? What relief (beyond unpaid wages) remains available to an employee suing directly under § 181.101 via § 181.171?

questions.title: What is the statutory basis and Article III redressability for a private plaintiff to seek MFLSA civil penalties that are payable only to the Commissioner?
questions.question_body: The panel notes both sides agree MFLSA statutory penalties are paid to the Commissioner, not to Cohen, yet suggests penalties might still afford redress under Laidlaw if the unlawful policy continues. Which MFLSA provision actually authorizes a private plaintiff to seek imposition of those state-payable penalties? If the money goes to the state, how is redressability satisfied for the private plaintiff’s injury? How do differences between Laidlaw’s federal citizen-suit structure and Minnesota’s MFLSA enforcement scheme affect the standing analysis?

questions.title: On remand, who bears the burden to prove mootness via voluntary cessation, and what evidence would make it “absolutely clear” Consilio’s overtime policy won’t recur?
questions.question_body: The court vacates the MFLSA ruling and remands to determine whether Cohen’s penalties claim is moot if Consilio ended its policy and it is “absolutely clear” the conduct will not recur. My understanding is that the defendant bears a heavy burden under the voluntary cessation doctrine. Is that the standard the district court should apply here? What kinds of proof (formal policy rescission, sworn declarations, duration of compliance, operational changes, audits, etc.) typically satisfy or fail the “absolutely clear” requirement in wage-and-hour disputes?

questions.title: Does the Minnesota Wage Theft Act (Minn. Stat. § 181.032) provide a private right to civil penalties for failure to give written notice of pay changes?
questions.question_body: The panel affirms dismissal of Cohen’s MWTA claim for lack of statutory authority to recover civil penalties. Section 181.032(d)(4) requires written notice of pay changes, and I thought enforcement could run through MFLSA § 177.27 (at least for the Commissioner). Is there any private remedy (damages, statutory penalties, or injunctive relief) for a § 181.032 notice violation, or is enforcement exclusively via the Commissioner? If a private remedy exists, what is it and where is it found?

questions.title: Did Cohen need to amend his complaint to seek rescission of the 2019 policy, or could the court have granted that different injunction at summary judgment under Rule 54(c)?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Cohen first requested rescission of the 2019 overtime policy in summary judgment briefing and that the district court properly declined to consider it, citing the principle that new claims must be raised via amendment. But Rule 54(c) allows courts to grant the relief a party is entitled to even if not demanded in the pleadings. In the Eighth Circuit, when is a change in requested injunctive relief treated as a new claim requiring amendment versus a permissible reconfiguration of remedies? Was Cohen’s rescission request a new claim or merely a different form of relief for the same violation?

questions.title: What is the effect of paying the named plaintiff in full on putative class claims that were never certified in this Minnesota wage case?
questions.question_body: Cohen filed on behalf of a putative class, but before certification Consilio paid him all claimed overtime and MFLSA liquidated damages, and the parties stipulated he’d been paid in full (leaving only penalties and injunctive relief at issue). The opinion doesn’t address the putative class. Under Genesis Healthcare and Campbell-Ewald, does full payment to an individual plaintiff in a pre-certification Minnesota wage case moot the putative class claims? Does it matter that this was an actual payment accepted via stipulation rather than an unaccepted Rule 68 offer?

questions.title: Can the court affirm merits rulings on MPWA/MWTA while remanding MFLSA for a jurisdictional determination, or must all merits await a global Article III analysis?
questions.question_body: The panel affirms on MPWA and MWTA but vacates and remands MFLSA to determine mootness. If Article III jurisdiction is uncertain post-payment, does Steel Co. require resolving jurisdiction before any merits ruling? Is it proper to decide the merits of some claims while remanding another for a jurisdictional inquiry because standing/mootness is assessed claim-by-claim, or does the employer’s payments potentially undermine jurisdiction across all claims?

questions.title: What is the legal effect of the concurrence’s statement about vacating attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest when the majority is silent?
questions.question_body: Judge Kobes states he “also vacate[s] the district court’s ruling as to attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest,” but the majority opinion does not mention those items. Does a separate concurrence alter the judgment or mandate in any way, or are fees/costs/interest unaffected unless addressed by the majority disposition? If the MFLSA penalties claim is found moot on remand, how should the district court handle requests for attorney’s fees under Minnesota wage statutes or other fee-shifting provisions?
